schema_sql: CREATE TABLE parcels (row_id BIGINT NOT NULL, weight_kg BIGINT NOT NULL)
original_sql: SELECT row_id FROM parcels WHERE weight_kg >= 15 AND weight_kg <= 15
reference_sql: SELECT row_id FROM parcels WHERE weight_kg = 15
derivation: The two inclusive bounds pin weight_kg to 15. Both parcels with that weight qualify.
source: SQL_Predicate_Family_Examples.sql, B3. Adapted from Apache Calcite RexProgramTest.java, https://github.com/apache/calcite/blob/57ad4ffb1ed9b86d18fcfd7627fdf5c4227bc172/core/src/test/java/org/apache/calcite/rex/RexProgramTest.java#L1078-L1079
error_exposed: Keeping only weight_kg >= 15 includes row 3 (weight 16). Keeping only weight_kg <= 15 includes row 1 (weight 14).

schema_sql: CREATE TABLE readings (row_id BIGINT NOT NULL, x BIGINT NOT NULL)
original_sql: SELECT row_id FROM readings WHERE NOT (x >= -2 AND x <= -2)
reference_sql: SELECT row_id FROM readings WHERE x != -2
derivation: Team variant of B3-01. The two inclusive bounds pin x to -2; negation excludes that point.
source: SQL_Predicate_Family_Examples.sql, B3
error_exposed: Returning TRUE incorrectly includes row 2.

schema_sql: CREATE TABLE pinned_ranges (row_id BIGINT NOT NULL, x BIGINT NOT NULL)
original_sql: SELECT row_id FROM pinned_ranges WHERE (x >= -4 AND x <= -4) OR (x >= 2 AND x <= 5)
reference_sql: SELECT row_id FROM pinned_ranges WHERE x = -4 OR (x >= 2 AND x <= 5)
derivation: The two inclusive bounds in the first OR branch pin x to -4, so that branch is equivalent to x = -4. Replacing only that branch preserves the separate inclusive interval from 2 through 5.
source: Team-derived variant of SQL_Predicate_Family_Examples.sql, B3 (B3-01), with a separate live interval.
error_exposed: Keeping only x >= 2 AND x <= 5 loses row 2 (x = -4). Keeping only x = -4 loses rows 5, 6 and 7 (x = 2, 3 and 5).

schema_sql: CREATE TABLE pinned_controls (row_id BIGINT NOT NULL, x BIGINT NOT NULL, y BIGINT NOT NULL)
original_sql: SELECT row_id FROM pinned_controls WHERE (x >= -3 AND x <= -3) AND y >= 10
reference_sql: SELECT row_id FROM pinned_controls WHERE x = -3 AND y >= 10
derivation: The two inclusive bounds pin x to -3. Replacing their conjunction with x = -3 preserves the independent requirement y >= 10; both conditions must still hold.
source: Team-derived variant of SQL_Predicate_Family_Examples.sql, B3 (B3-01), retaining an independent comparison on a second column.
error_exposed: Returning only x = -3 drops y >= 10 and incorrectly includes rows 2 and 6 (y = 9 and 0).

schema_sql: CREATE TABLE accounts (row_id BIGINT NOT NULL, balance_cents BIGINT NOT NULL)
original_sql: SELECT row_id FROM accounts WHERE balance_cents >= 0 AND balance_cents != 0
reference_sql: SELECT row_id FROM accounts WHERE balance_cents > 0
derivation: For every non-null BIGINT balance_cents, being at least zero and unequal to zero is equivalent to being strictly positive. The excluded endpoint changes the inclusive lower bound to a strict one.
source: SQL_Predicate_Family_Examples.sql, B4. Rule instance from PostgreSQL 17, sections 8.17.3 and 8.17.7, https://www.postgresql.org/docs/17/rangetypes.html
error_exposed: Keeping only balance_cents >= 0 incorrectly includes row 2 (balance_cents = 0).

schema_sql: CREATE TABLE upper_endpoints (row_id BIGINT NOT NULL, x BIGINT NOT NULL)
original_sql: SELECT row_id FROM upper_endpoints WHERE x <= -2 AND x != -2
reference_sql: SELECT row_id FROM upper_endpoints WHERE x < -2
derivation: For every non-null BIGINT x, x <= -2 permits exactly the values below -2 together with -2 itself. Excluding that endpoint leaves exactly x < -2. This applies to an upper bound at a negative endpoint rather than the seed's lower bound.
source: Team-derived variant of SQL_Predicate_Family_Examples.sql, B4 (B4-01), excluding a negative upper endpoint.
error_exposed: Keeping only x <= -2 incorrectly includes row 3 (x = -2), the excluded upper endpoint.

schema_sql: CREATE TABLE bounded_endpoints (row_id BIGINT NOT NULL, x BIGINT NOT NULL)
original_sql: SELECT row_id FROM bounded_endpoints WHERE x >= -2 AND x <= 3 AND x != -2
reference_sql: SELECT row_id FROM bounded_endpoints WHERE x > -2 AND x <= 3
derivation: For every non-null BIGINT x, the conjunction x >= -2 AND x != -2 is equivalent to x > -2. Conjoining the unchanged upper bound x <= 3 on both sides preserves equivalence and keeps the upper endpoint included.
source: Team-derived variant of SQL_Predicate_Family_Examples.sql, B4 (B4-01), excluding one endpoint of a two-sided interval.
error_exposed: Returning only x > -2 drops x <= 3 and incorrectly includes row 6 (x = 4).

schema_sql: CREATE TABLE endpoint_branches (row_id BIGINT NOT NULL, x BIGINT NOT NULL, y BIGINT NOT NULL)
original_sql: SELECT row_id FROM endpoint_branches WHERE (x >= 0 AND x != 0) OR y = 7
reference_sql: SELECT row_id FROM endpoint_branches WHERE x > 0 OR y = 7
derivation: For every legal row, x >= 0 AND x != 0 is equivalent to x > 0. Replacing only that OR branch leaves the independent y = 7 branch unchanged, so rows with y = 7 still qualify even when x is zero or negative.
source: Team-derived variant of SQL_Predicate_Family_Examples.sql, B4 (B4-01), retaining an independent live OR branch on a second column.
error_exposed: Returning only x > 0 drops the live y = 7 branch and loses rows 4 and 5 (x = -1 and 0 with y = 7).

schema_sql: CREATE TABLE counters (row_id BIGINT NOT NULL, counter_value BIGINT NOT NULL)
original_sql: SELECT row_id FROM counters WHERE counter_value <= 9223372036854775807
reference_sql: SELECT row_id FROM counters WHERE TRUE
derivation: Every legal counter_value is a non-null signed BIGINT and therefore at most 9223372036854775807. The original predicate is true on every legal row and is equivalent to TRUE over the complete declared type domain.
source: SQL_Predicate_Family_Examples.sql, B5. Adapted from MySQL 8.4 Reference Manual, section 10.2.1.14, Constant-Folding Optimization, https://dev.mysql.com/doc/refman/8.4/en/constant-folding-optimization.html
error_exposed: Using counter_value < 9223372036854775807 instead of TRUE loses row 5 at the signed BIGINT maximum.

schema_sql: CREATE TABLE minimum_bounds (row_id BIGINT NOT NULL, x BIGINT NOT NULL)
original_sql: SELECT row_id FROM minimum_bounds WHERE x >= -9223372036854775808
reference_sql: SELECT row_id FROM minimum_bounds WHERE TRUE
derivation: Every non-null signed BIGINT x is at least -9223372036854775808. The inclusive lower-bound predicate therefore holds for every legal row, including the signed minimum itself, and is equivalent to TRUE across the entire type domain.
source: Team-derived variant of SQL_Predicate_Family_Examples.sql, B5 (B5-01), using the signed minimum lower bound and its adjacent value.
error_exposed: Returning x > -9223372036854775808 changes the inclusive type bound to a strict bound and loses row 1 at the signed BIGINT minimum.

schema_sql: CREATE TABLE impossible_bounds (row_id BIGINT NOT NULL, x BIGINT NOT NULL)
original_sql: SELECT row_id FROM impossible_bounds WHERE x > 9223372036854775807
reference_sql: SELECT row_id FROM impossible_bounds WHERE FALSE
derivation: No legal signed BIGINT x exceeds 9223372036854775807. The strict comparison with the in-range maximum is false on every legal row, so it is equivalent to FALSE without using an out-of-range SQL literal.
source: Team-derived variant of SQL_Predicate_Family_Examples.sql, B5 (B5-01), turning the maximum type limit into an impossible strict comparison.
error_exposed: Returning x >= 9223372036854775807 incorrectly includes row 5 at the signed BIGINT maximum even though the original selects no row.

schema_sql: CREATE TABLE bounded_controls (row_id BIGINT NOT NULL, x BIGINT NOT NULL, y BIGINT NOT NULL)
original_sql: SELECT row_id FROM bounded_controls WHERE x <= 9223372036854775807 AND y >= 10
reference_sql: SELECT row_id FROM bounded_controls WHERE y >= 10
derivation: The signed BIGINT type makes x <= 9223372036854775807 true on every legal row. Its conjunction with y >= 10 is therefore equivalent to y >= 10. The independent restriction on y remains necessary regardless of whether x is at its minimum, maximum or an interior value.
source: Team-derived variant of SQL_Predicate_Family_Examples.sql, B5 (B5-01), conjoining the guaranteed type bound with an independent restriction on a second column.
error_exposed: Keeping only x <= 9223372036854775807 drops y >= 10 and incorrectly includes rows 1 and 4 (y = 9 at the minimum and maximum x values).

schema_sql: CREATE TABLE samples (row_id BIGINT NOT NULL, reading BIGINT NOT NULL)
original_sql: SELECT row_id FROM samples WHERE (reading >= 10 AND reading <= 20) OR (reading >= 18 AND reading <= 25) OR reading >= 40
reference_sql: SELECT row_id FROM samples WHERE (reading >= 10 AND reading <= 25) OR reading >= 40
derivation: The inclusive intervals [10, 20] and [18, 25] overlap, so their union is [10, 25]. The separate interval starting at 40 also qualifies.
source: SQL_Predicate_Family_Examples.sql, C1. Adapted from Apache Calcite RexProgramTest.java, https://github.com/apache/calcite/blob/57ad4ffb1ed9b86d18fcfd7627fdf5c4227bc172/core/src/test/java/org/apache/calcite/rex/RexProgramTest.java#L1619-L1635
error_exposed: Dropping reading >= 40 loses row 10 (reading 40). Extending the merged interval through the gap incorrectly includes row 8 (26) or row 9 (39).

schema_sql: CREATE TABLE chained_ranges (row_id BIGINT NOT NULL, x BIGINT NOT NULL)
original_sql: SELECT row_id FROM chained_ranges WHERE (x >= 0 AND x <= 4) OR (x >= 3 AND x <= 7) OR (x >= 6 AND x <= 10)
reference_sql: SELECT row_id FROM chained_ranges WHERE x >= 0 AND x <= 10
derivation: The inclusive intervals [0, 4] and [3, 7] overlap, and [3, 7] also overlaps [6, 10]. Their complete chain therefore covers exactly [0, 10], even though the first and third intervals do not overlap directly. The lower and upper endpoints remain included.
source: Team-derived variant of data/SQL_Predicate_Family_Examples.sql, family C1 seed (C1-01): extend the overlap merge to a chain of three intervals.
error_exposed: Returning WHERE x >= 0 AND x <= 7 merges only the first two intervals and drops the third interval's uncovered tail: row 8 (x = 8) and row 9 (x = 10) are incorrectly missing. Rows 1 (x = -1) and 10 (x = 11) check that the complete merge does not extend past its endpoints.

schema_sql: CREATE TABLE separated_ranges (row_id BIGINT NOT NULL, x BIGINT NOT NULL)
original_sql: SELECT row_id FROM separated_ranges WHERE (x >= -4 AND x <= 0) OR (x >= -1 AND x <= 3) OR (x >= 5 AND x <= 7)
reference_sql: SELECT row_id FROM separated_ranges WHERE (x >= -4 AND x <= 3) OR (x >= 5 AND x <= 7)
derivation: The inclusive intervals [-4, 0] and [-1, 3] overlap and combine into [-4, 3]. The independent interval [5, 7] must survive. The integer 4 is the one-point gap between those two resulting intervals and remains excluded.
source: Team-derived variant of data/SQL_Predicate_Family_Examples.sql, family C1 seed (C1-01): merge negative-endpoint overlapping intervals while preserving a separate interval across a one-integer gap.
error_exposed: Returning WHERE x >= -4 AND x <= 7 incorrectly fills the one-integer gap and includes row 6 (x = 4). Returning only WHERE x >= -4 AND x <= 3 drops the surviving separate interval and incorrectly misses row 7 (x = 5), row 8 (x = 6), and row 9 (x = 7). Rows 1 and 10 test the values immediately outside the complete union.

schema_sql: CREATE TABLE guarded_ranges (row_id BIGINT NOT NULL, reading BIGINT NOT NULL, enabled BIGINT NOT NULL)
original_sql: SELECT row_id FROM guarded_ranges WHERE (enabled = 1 AND ((reading >= 10 AND reading <= 15) OR (reading >= 14 AND reading <= 20))) OR reading >= 40
reference_sql: SELECT row_id FROM guarded_ranges WHERE (enabled = 1 AND reading >= 10 AND reading <= 20) OR reading >= 40
derivation: Inside the enabled = 1 branch, the inclusive intervals [10, 15] and [14, 20] overlap and combine into [10, 20]. The same enabled guard must still restrict that merged interval. The separate reading >= 40 branch is independent of enabled and must remain available for every enabled value.
source: Team-derived variant of data/SQL_Predicate_Family_Examples.sql, family C1 seed (C1-01): merge intervals within a branch guarded by a second column while retaining an independent tail branch.
error_exposed: Returning WHERE (reading >= 10 AND reading <= 20) OR reading >= 40 drops the enabled = 1 guard and incorrectly includes row 4 (reading = 14, enabled = 0) and row 11 (reading = 10, enabled = 0). Dropping the independent reading >= 40 branch loses rows 9 and 10. Applying enabled = 1 to that tail as well incorrectly loses row 9 (reading = 40, enabled = 0). Rows 1, 7, and 8 retain the exclusions below, just above, and between the accepted intervals.

schema_sql: CREATE TABLE jobs (row_id BIGINT NOT NULL, stage BIGINT NOT NULL)
original_sql: SELECT row_id FROM jobs WHERE stage = 4 OR stage = 5 OR stage = 6
reference_sql: SELECT row_id FROM jobs WHERE stage >= 4 AND stage <= 6
derivation: The only integer values in the inclusive interval [4, 6] are 4, 5, and 6. Listing those three consecutive stages and testing the two inclusive bounds therefore select exactly the same legal rows.
source: data/SQL_Predicate_Family_Examples.sql, C2 seed. Rule instance of adjacency in a discrete integer domain; PostgreSQL 17, sections 8.17.3 and 8.17.7 on endpoints and discrete ranges, https://www.postgresql.org/docs/17/rangetypes.html
error_exposed: Using strict bounds stage > 4 AND stage < 6 loses row 2 (stage = 4) and row 4 (stage = 6). Rows 1 (stage = 3) and 5 (stage = 7) check the adjacent excluded values.

schema_sql: CREATE TABLE negative_stages (row_id BIGINT NOT NULL, x BIGINT NOT NULL)
original_sql: SELECT row_id FROM negative_stages WHERE x = -5 OR x = -4 OR x = -3 OR x = -2
reference_sql: SELECT row_id FROM negative_stages WHERE x >= -5 AND x <= -2
derivation: The four listed negative values are consecutive integers. Their union is exactly the inclusive interval [-5, -2], with no intermediate integer omitted. Both negative endpoints must remain included; the adjacent integers -6 and -1 remain excluded.
source: Team-derived variant of data/SQL_Predicate_Family_Examples.sql, family C2 seed (C2-01): extend the three-point list to four consecutive negative integers.
error_exposed: Returning WHERE x > -5 AND x < -2 replaces the inclusive endpoints with strict bounds and incorrectly misses row 2 (x = -5) and row 5 (x = -2). Rows 1 and 6 also expose a range widened beyond the listed negative values.

schema_sql: CREATE TABLE stages_with_outlier (row_id BIGINT NOT NULL, x BIGINT NOT NULL)
original_sql: SELECT row_id FROM stages_with_outlier WHERE x = 2 OR x = 3 OR x = 4 OR x = 9
reference_sql: SELECT row_id FROM stages_with_outlier WHERE (x >= 2 AND x <= 4) OR x = 9
derivation: Only 2, 3, and 4 form a consecutive run, so those three equalities can become the inclusive interval [2, 4]. The isolated value 9 remains a separate equality. Values in the gap between 4 and 9 are not in the original list and must stay excluded.
source: Team-derived variant of data/SQL_Predicate_Family_Examples.sql, family C2 seed (C2-01): retain one isolated point beside a consecutive run.
error_exposed: Returning WHERE x >= 2 AND x <= 9 incorrectly bridges the gap and includes row 5 (x = 5) and row 6 (x = 8). Returning only WHERE x >= 2 AND x <= 4 drops the isolated live alternative and incorrectly misses row 7 (x = 9).

schema_sql: CREATE TABLE excluded_stages (row_id BIGINT NOT NULL, x BIGINT NOT NULL)
original_sql: SELECT row_id FROM excluded_stages WHERE NOT (x = -2 OR x = -1 OR x = 0)
reference_sql: SELECT row_id FROM excluded_stages WHERE NOT (x >= -2 AND x <= 0)
derivation: The three listed points are exactly the integers in the inclusive interval [-2, 0]. Negating either representation selects precisely the integers outside that interval. In particular, both listed endpoints are excluded, while their immediately adjacent outside values are selected.
source: Team-derived variant of data/SQL_Predicate_Family_Examples.sql, family C2 seed (C2-01): simplify a consecutive run beneath NOT while preserving its inclusive endpoints.
error_exposed: Returning WHERE NOT (x > -2 AND x < 0) uses strict inner bounds and incorrectly includes row 2 (x = -2) and row 4 (x = 0). Rows 1 (x = -3) and 5 (x = 1) check that the complement retains both sides of the excluded run.

schema_sql: CREATE TABLE inventory (row_id BIGINT NOT NULL, stock_delta BIGINT NOT NULL)
original_sql: SELECT row_id FROM inventory WHERE stock_delta < 0 OR stock_delta > 0
reference_sql: SELECT row_id FROM inventory WHERE stock_delta != 0
derivation: Every non-null integer is below zero, equal to zero, or above zero. The two strict ranges cover exactly the nonzero values, so their union is equivalent to stock_delta != 0.
source: data/SQL_Predicate_Family_Examples.sql, C3 seed. Test-input adaptation from SQLGlot optimizer tests, simplify.sql, Comparisons section, https://github.com/tobymao/sqlglot/blob/main/tests/fixtures/optimizer/simplify.sql . SQLGlot's expected expression retains the two comparisons; the smaller stock_delta != 0 reference is supplied by the team, not taken as SQLGlot's expected rewrite.
error_exposed: Returning WHERE TRUE incorrectly includes row 2 (stock_delta = 0), the one-point gap. Keeping only stock_delta < 0 loses row 3, and keeping only stock_delta > 0 loses row 1, so both live ranges have sample coverage.

schema_sql: CREATE TABLE isolated_gap (row_id BIGINT NOT NULL, x BIGINT NOT NULL)
original_sql: SELECT row_id FROM isolated_gap WHERE NOT (x < 4 OR x > 4)
reference_sql: SELECT row_id FROM isolated_gap WHERE x = 4
derivation: The inner union selects all integers except 4. Negating that union reverses the one-point gap into the only selected point, so the complete predicate is equivalent to x = 4.
source: Team-derived variant of data/SQL_Predicate_Family_Examples.sql, family C3 seed (C3-01): negate the two-range union to select its single missing point. The reference is a team derivation.
error_exposed: Returning WHERE x != 4 forgets the outer NOT: it incorrectly misses row 2 (x = 4) and includes row 1 (x = 3) and row 3 (x = 5). The samples cover the missing point and its immediate neighbors on both sides.

schema_sql: CREATE TABLE guarded_gap (row_id BIGINT NOT NULL, x BIGINT NOT NULL, enabled BIGINT NOT NULL)
original_sql: SELECT row_id FROM guarded_gap WHERE (x < 0 OR x > 0) AND enabled = 1
reference_sql: SELECT row_id FROM guarded_gap WHERE x != 0 AND enabled = 1
derivation: The strict ranges on x together exclude only zero. Replacing that union with x != 0 preserves its truth value, but the independent enabled = 1 conjunct must still hold. This equivalence does not restrict the legal BIGINT domain of enabled to the two sampled values.
source: Team-derived variant of data/SQL_Predicate_Family_Examples.sql, family C3 seed (C3-01): simplify a one-point gap while retaining a condition on a second column. The reference is a team derivation.
error_exposed: Returning WHERE x != 0 drops the enabled = 1 restriction and incorrectly includes row 4 (x = -1, enabled = 0) and row 5 (x = 1, enabled = 0). Row 2 checks that zero stays excluded even when the guard holds, and rows 1 and 3 preserve the two live sides of the gap.

schema_sql: CREATE TABLE windowed_gap (row_id BIGINT NOT NULL, x BIGINT NOT NULL)
original_sql: SELECT row_id FROM windowed_gap WHERE (x >= -3 AND x <= 3) AND (x < 0 OR x > 0)
reference_sql: SELECT row_id FROM windowed_gap WHERE x >= -3 AND x <= 3 AND x != 0
derivation: Within the inclusive window [-3, 3], the strict ranges x < 0 and x > 0 exclude exactly zero. Replacing that union with x != 0 is valid only while keeping both outer window bounds, so the complete result remains the bounded window with one point removed.
source: Team-derived variant of data/SQL_Predicate_Family_Examples.sql, family C3 seed (C3-01): place the one-point gap inside an inclusive bounded window. The reference is a team derivation.
error_exposed: Returning WHERE x != 0 drops the window and incorrectly includes row 1 (x = -4) and row 7 (x = 4). Returning only WHERE x >= -3 AND x <= 3 fills the gap and incorrectly includes row 4 (x = 0). Rows 2 and 6 ensure both window endpoints survive, and rows 3 and 5 retain the immediate neighbors of the excluded point.

schema_sql: CREATE TABLE bookings (row_id BIGINT NOT NULL, lead_days BIGINT NOT NULL)
original_sql: SELECT row_id FROM bookings WHERE (lead_days <= 2 OR lead_days >= 9) AND lead_days >= 5
reference_sql: SELECT row_id FROM bookings WHERE lead_days >= 9
derivation: The outer condition lead_days >= 5 rules out the branch lead_days <= 2. Every value satisfying the surviving lead_days >= 9 branch already satisfies the outer condition, so that branch alone selects exactly the same legal rows.
source: data/SQL_Predicate_Family_Examples.sql, C4 seed. Rule instance of range intersection from PostgreSQL 17, section 9.20: https://www.postgresql.org/docs/17/functions-range.html
error_exposed: Returning only lead_days >= 5 incorrectly includes row 3 (lead_days = 5) and row 4 (lead_days = 8). Returning lead_days > 9 incorrectly loses row 5 at the surviving inclusive endpoint.

schema_sql: CREATE TABLE upper_cut (row_id BIGINT NOT NULL, x BIGINT NOT NULL)
original_sql: SELECT row_id FROM upper_cut WHERE ((x >= -5 AND x <= -1) OR x >= 4) AND x <= 2
reference_sql: SELECT row_id FROM upper_cut WHERE x >= -5 AND x <= -1
derivation: The outer upper bound x <= 2 makes the x >= 4 branch impossible. Every value in the bounded left interval [-5, -1] already satisfies that upper bound, so the complete bounded interval remains unchanged, including both endpoints.
source: Team-derived variant of data/SQL_Predicate_Family_Examples.sql, C4 seed (C4-01): use an outer upper bound to remove the right branch while preserving a finite left interval.
error_exposed: Returning the uncut union (x >= -5 AND x <= -1) OR x >= 4 ignores the outer upper bound and incorrectly includes rows 8 and 9 (x = 4 and 5). Returning only x <= -1 after removing the right branch drops the retained lower endpoint requirement and incorrectly includes row 1 (x = -6).

schema_sql: CREATE TABLE surviving_ranges (row_id BIGINT NOT NULL, x BIGINT NOT NULL)
original_sql: SELECT row_id FROM surviving_ranges WHERE (x <= -4 OR (x >= 0 AND x <= 2) OR (x >= 6 AND x <= 9)) AND x >= -1
reference_sql: SELECT row_id FROM surviving_ranges WHERE (x >= 0 AND x <= 2) OR (x >= 6 AND x <= 9)
derivation: The outer lower bound x >= -1 removes the x <= -4 branch. Both finite intervals [0, 2] and [6, 9] already imply x >= -1, so both survive intact. Their intervening gap remains excluded.
source: Team-derived variant of data/SQL_Predicate_Family_Examples.sql, C4 seed (C4-01): an outer bound removes one of three branches and preserves two disjoint finite intervals.
error_exposed: Keeping only x >= 6 AND x <= 9 incorrectly loses rows 4, 5 and 6 from the other surviving interval. Replacing the survivors by x >= 0 AND x <= 9 incorrectly includes rows 7 and 8 (x = 3 and 5) in the gap.

schema_sql: CREATE TABLE clipped_range (row_id BIGINT NOT NULL, x BIGINT NOT NULL)
original_sql: SELECT row_id FROM clipped_range WHERE (x <= -5 OR (x >= 1 AND x <= 10)) AND x >= 4
reference_sql: SELECT row_id FROM clipped_range WHERE x >= 4 AND x <= 10
derivation: The outer lower bound x >= 4 eliminates the x <= -5 branch and intersects the surviving interval [1, 10] with [4, maximum BIGINT]. The result is exactly [4, 10], with the original upper endpoint still required.
source: Team-derived variant of data/SQL_Predicate_Family_Examples.sql, C4 seed (C4-01): the outer bound both eliminates a branch and clips the lower end of the survivor.
error_exposed: Returning x >= 1 AND x <= 10 only removes the impossible branch but fails to clip the survivor, incorrectly including rows 5 and 6 (x = 1 and 3). Returning only x >= 4 also includes row 10 (x = 11) beyond the retained upper endpoint.

schema_sql: CREATE TABLE measurements (row_id BIGINT NOT NULL, reading BIGINT NOT NULL)
original_sql: SELECT row_id FROM measurements WHERE ((reading > 0 AND reading <= 8) OR reading >= 14) AND reading != 4 AND reading != 11
reference_sql: SELECT row_id FROM measurements WHERE ((reading > 0 AND reading <= 8) OR reading >= 14) AND reading != 4
derivation: The union admits values greater than 0 through 8 and values at least 14, so it already rejects 11 in the gap. The reading != 11 comparison is redundant. The reading != 4 comparison must remain because 4 belongs to the first live interval.
source: data/SQL_Predicate_Family_Examples.sql, C5 seed. Test adaptation of Apache Calcite RexProgramTest.java, testSimplifyRange, commit 57ad4ff: https://github.com/apache/calcite/blob/57ad4ffb1ed9b86d18fcfd7627fdf5c4227bc172/core/src/test/java/org/apache/calcite/rex/RexProgramTest.java#L1589-L1605
error_exposed: Removing both exclusions incorrectly includes row 4 (reading = 4). Filling the gap between the two live intervals incorrectly admits rows 7, 8 and 9 (reading = 9, 11 and 13).

schema_sql: CREATE TABLE double_gap (row_id BIGINT NOT NULL, x BIGINT NOT NULL)
original_sql: SELECT row_id FROM double_gap WHERE ((x >= 0 AND x <= 3) OR (x >= 8 AND x <= 10)) AND x != 5 AND x != 6
reference_sql: SELECT row_id FROM double_gap WHERE (x >= 0 AND x <= 3) OR (x >= 8 AND x <= 10)
derivation: The finite intervals [0, 3] and [8, 10] exclude every value from 4 through 7. Both 5 and 6 therefore fail the union already, so both explicit exclusions can be removed while retaining both interval boundaries.
source: Team-derived variant of data/SQL_Predicate_Family_Examples.sql, C5 seed (C5-01): remove two exclusions inside one gap between finite live intervals.
error_exposed: Replacing the union with x >= 0 AND x <= 10 fills its gap and incorrectly includes rows 4, 5, 6 and 7 (x = 4, 5, 6 and 7). Keeping only the first interval loses rows 8 and 9 from the other live interval.

schema_sql: CREATE TABLE excluded_branches (row_id BIGINT NOT NULL, x BIGINT NOT NULL)
original_sql: SELECT row_id FROM excluded_branches WHERE (((x >= -4 AND x <= 0) AND x != -2) OR ((x >= 6 AND x <= 10) AND x != 8)) AND x != 3
reference_sql: SELECT row_id FROM excluded_branches WHERE ((x >= -4 AND x <= 0) AND x != -2) OR ((x >= 6 AND x <= 10) AND x != 8)
derivation: The first branch is contained in [-4, 0] and the second in [6, 10], so neither can admit 3 in the intervening gap. Only the outer x != 3 condition is redundant. The branch-local exclusions at -2 and 8 each remove a value from a live interval and must both remain.
source: Team-derived variant of data/SQL_Predicate_Family_Examples.sql, C5 seed (C5-01): retain two distinct branch-local meaningful exclusions while deleting an outer gap exclusion.
error_exposed: Dropping the first branch-local x != -2 while preserving the other exclusion incorrectly includes row 4 (x = -2). Dropping the second branch-local x != 8 instead incorrectly includes row 12 (x = 8). The gap witness row 8 (x = 3) remains excluded after removing only the redundant outer condition.

schema_sql: CREATE TABLE local_gap (row_id BIGINT NOT NULL, x BIGINT NOT NULL, enabled BIGINT NOT NULL)
original_sql: SELECT row_id FROM local_gap WHERE ((x <= -2 OR x >= 4) AND x != 1) OR enabled = 1
reference_sql: SELECT row_id FROM local_gap WHERE (x <= -2 OR x >= 4) OR enabled = 1
derivation: Within the first branch, x <= -2 OR x >= 4 already rejects 1, so its local x != 1 is redundant. The enabled = 1 branch is independent and can admit x = 1; removing the local exclusion preserves that branch, whereas moving it outside the OR would change the query.
source: Team-derived variant of data/SQL_Predicate_Family_Examples.sql, C5 seed (C5-01): a redundant exclusion is scoped to one branch while a second-column branch can admit the same gap value.
error_exposed: Hoisting x != 1 to the whole query, as ((x <= -2 OR x >= 4) OR enabled = 1) AND x != 1, incorrectly loses row 5 (x = 1, enabled = 1). Dropping the independent enabled branch loses rows 5 and 9. Rows 4 and 5 have the same x = 1 but different enabled values and must have different outcomes.
